questions.prompt: What is a fork on GitHub?

options.text: A branch inside the original repository
A server-side copy of a repository under your own account
A backup tag of a release

questions.explanation: A fork is your own copy of someone else's repository on GitHub. You have push access to your fork even without access to the original.

questions.prompt: In the fork-and-pull model, what does the `upstream` remote point to?

options.text: The original repository you forked from

questions.explanation: By convention, origin is your fork and upstream is the original repository — the source you sync from and open pull requests against.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the fork-and-pull workflow are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Forking creates a copy of the repo under your account
You clone your fork, so origin points to it
You add upstream to sync with the original
You need write access to the original repo to contribute

questions.explanation: Forking copies the repo to your account, origin is your fork, and upstream lets you sync. You do NOT need write access to the original — that's the whole point of forking.

questions.prompt: To add the original repository as a remote so you can sync, run: git remote add ________ <original-url>
questions.explanation: By convention the original repo is added as the remote named upstream, distinct from origin (your fork).

questions.prompt: Your fork's main has fallen behind the original. How do you update it?

options.text: Delete the fork and fork again
git fetch upstream, then merge (or rebase) upstream/main into your main, and push to your fork
git push --force to the upstream repository
There is no way to sync a fork

questions.explanation: Fetch the upstream, integrate upstream/main into your main, and push to origin (your fork). This keeps your fork current without re-forking.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role.

pairs.right: A copy of a repo under your account
Propose your changes back to upstream

questions.explanation: A fork copies the repo to your account; origin is your fork; upstream is the source; a PR proposes your work back to it.
